justification_text:
The point estimates for each time horizon—1 day, 1 week, and 1 month—were driven by the same central assumption about the expected value. Specifically, the point estimate is 261.41 across all horizons because it represents our best prediction of the most likely outcome based on fundamental data, historical trends, or an underlying model. This consistency suggests that while the central forecast remains stable over time, the uncertainty about where the actual value will land grows as the time horizon extends.

The confidence intervals widen as we move from 1 day to 1 month because uncertainty accumulates over time. In the near term (1 day), we might expect fewer variables to impact the outcome, making predictions more precise. As the time horizon extends to 1 week or 1 month, additional factors—such as market volatility, unforeseen events, or compounding small errors in the forecast—introduce greater uncertainty. This is why the range of potential outcomes (the confidence intervals) becomes broader, reflecting heightened difficulty in being precise as time goes on.

Certain risks or events could push outcomes outside these intervals, though the 90% confidence level accounts for most typical scenarios. Unplanned disruptions—such as major geopolitical events, sudden changes in economic conditions, unexpected regulatory announcements, or even extreme market behavior—could produce outcomes far beyond the forecasted range. For example, a shock of this nature could significantly alter the trajectory of the underlying variables we used to build this forecast. While we aim to encapsulate most variability in our intervals, extreme risks and tail events remain unpredictable by their very nature.
